articles.title: Social media data collection: A 2026 guide
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Social media data collection is the process of gathering performance metrics, audience information, and public conversation data from social platforms to inform marketing strategy.
  2. The most valuable data to track depends on your goals, but enterprise teams should prioritize engagement, sentiment, conversions, competitive share of voice, and reach.
  3. Effective collection combines analytics tools, social listening, surveys, community engagement, competitor analysis, and API integrations.
  4. Compliance with GDPR, CCPA, and platform terms of service is a legal requirement for any organization collecting social media data.

What is social media data?

Social media data collection is the process of gathering information from social media platforms about your audience, content, and performance. Most social media data collection programs pull from two buckets, and knowing the difference matters for both strategy and compliance.

First-party data comes from accounts you own and manage. That includes impressions, clicks, reach, and follower growth pulled from social media analytics tools, plus the audience information platforms share with you as the page owner.

Publicly available data is everything happening outside your own channels: posts, comments, hashtags, reviews, and mentions across the wider platform. You can track that kind of data using social listening tools. It is what people say when they are not talking to you directly, which often makes it the more honest signal.

Both are valuable, and most social media data collection strategies use a mix of the two. Facebook alone has over three billion monthly active users, so even a narrow slice of public conversation can produce more data than a team can read manually.

This data helps you understand what’s happening on your channels, what’s resonating with your audience, and where you can improve.

Bonus !!!

What’s the difference between data collection, mining, and extraction?

Data collection, mining, and extraction are three key steps in using social media data effectively.

You can think of it like this:

  • Collection: Gathering
  • Mining: Analyzing
  • Extraction: Exporting or isolating the pieces you need

Each step plays a different role in turning raw numbers into decisions that actually help you grow.

What types of data do social platforms collect?

Social platforms collect far more data than they hand back to marketers, so it helps to know where the line sits. Platforms gather behavioral, demographic, device, and location signals to power their algorithms and ad products, then expose a filtered subset of that through analytics dashboards and APIs.

The broad categories platforms collect include:

  • Content interaction data: Views, watch time, likes, comments, shares, saves, and scroll behavior
  • Demographic data: Age range, gender, language, and self-reported profile details
  • Location data: Country, region, and city level signals, plus device location where users have opted in
  • Device and technical data: Device type, operating system, app version, and connection quality
  • Off-platform signals: Activity captured through advertising pixels, conversion APIs, and partner integrations

The data you can collect as a marketer is almost always aggregated and anonymized. You can see that 40% of your audience falls within a specific age bracket, but not who those individuals are. That distinction is the foundation of most privacy rules covered later in this guide.

articles.title: How to make money on TikTok in 2026: 15 proven ways
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. TikTok offers 15 proven ways to earn money in 2026, from native programs like the Creator Rewards Program and TikTok Pulse to brand partnerships, affiliate sales, and selling your own products or expertise.
  2. You don’t need a massive following to start. Affiliate marketing, the TikTok Rewards referral program, and TikTok Shop let creators and businesses earn with as few as 1,000 followers, and in some cases none at all.
  3. The most consistent TikTok income usually comes from stacking methods together, like pairing Creator Rewards with affiliate links and the occasional brand deal.

Can you really make money on TikTok?

Yes, creators and businesses do earn real money on TikTok, but the range is enormous. Some people make a few dollars a month from views alone, while others build full businesses on the back of TikTok Shop sales or brand deals. The difference usually comes down to how you monetize, not how many followers you have.

A few factors tend to decide where you land:

  • Your niche: Categories with products to sell or expertise to teach monetize faster than general entertainment.
  • Your consistency: Regular posting keeps you eligible for programs that require recent activity and gives the algorithm more to work with.
  • Your audience size and engagement: Some methods have follower minimums, and brands care as much about engagement as reach.
  • Your monetization mix: Relying on one income stream leaves you exposed when a program changes or a video underperforms.

The realistic takeaway: treat TikTok payouts from views as a bonus, and treat selling something (products, services, or someone else’s products through affiliate links) as the actual business.

What do you need to start earning on TikTok?

Most TikTok monetization features have their own eligibility bar, and they’re not all the same. Here’s how the major methods compare so you can spot the ones you already qualify for.

TikTok updates these requirements often, so check the relevant page in TikTok Studio or TikTok’s creator support documentation before you build a plan around any single feature.

How to make money on TikTok through native programs

TikTok has a handful of built-in ways to pay you without a brand or a product in the picture. These are the fastest to switch on, and most of them live in the Monetization section of TikTok Studio.

1. Join the Creator Rewards Program

Who can make money with this tactic: Creators

Want to get paid directly by TikTok when your videos go viral? Join the Creator Rewards Program.

Creator Rewards replaced TikTok’s Creator Fund to incentivize high-quality, original content creation. In this new version, the program pays out rewards for videos that:

  • Are at least one minute long
  • Get at least 1,000 views
  • Aren’t a Duet or Stitch
  • Aren’t created using Photo Mode
  • Follow the program’s rules and terms

To be eligible for TikTok Creator Rewards,

  • You must have a Personal TikTok account (Business accounts don’t qualify)
  • Your TikTok account must be registered in United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, South Korea, France, Mexico, or Brazil
  • You must have at least 10,000 followers and 100,000 video views in the last 30 days
  • Your account must be following TikTok’s Community Guidelines and Terms
  • Be at least 18 years of age

TikTok lists several factors used to calculate payouts on the Creator Rewards page, from originality to play duration. Payouts are calculated per 1,000 qualified views, which TikTok defines as views of at least five seconds on videos longer than one minute, so a video with a big view count and low watch time won’t earn much.

2. Earn gifts and tips from your audience

Who can make money with this tactic: Creators

Gifts are a way for viewers to show their appreciation to creators. Gifts from viewers turn into cash for you.

Here’s how it works:

  1. Users purchase coins from TikTok that they can use to buy virtual gifts.
  2. From there, users can send a gift to the creator when they watch a video they think is amazing.
  3. Creators convert their gifts into TikTok diamonds which they can cash out for real currency.

Two coins are worth one diamond, and one diamond is worth about $0.005, which means it takes 200 diamonds to earn $1. So a big, generous audience is really the only way gifts are going to work as a true financial opportunity.

What is a social media collaboration tool?

A social media collaboration tool is software that helps teams plan, create, review, approve, and publish content, all from one shared workspace.

It doesn’t just benefit marketing. The right tool brings marketing, creative, legal, and other stakeholders into the same workflow, with clear roles, approvals, and permissions (no more “who approved this?” moments).

In 2026, that definition has stretched. Gartner now treats social media management and listening as a single strategic market, and most platforms in this category layer AI-assisted drafting and routing on top of the workflow, which makes governance and audit trails just as important as the collaboration features themselves.

Why do social media teams need collaboration tools in 2026?

Social teams need collaboration tools because the work no longer sits with one person. Content volume, approval requirements, and real-time engagement all scale faster than headcount, and coordination is usually where things break first.

Here’s what makes cross-functional collaboration harder than it used to be:

  • More channels, more formats: A single campaign might need vertical video, carousels, community replies, and paid variants across the 6–7 platforms people visit monthly, each with different owners and timelines.
  • Tighter approval requirements: Regulated industries and large brands often need legal or compliance sign-off before anything publishes. Without structured routing, that review happens over email and gets lost.
  • Real-time engagement expectations: Comments and DMs need answers within hours, not days. That only works when multiple people can triage from a shared queue without duplicating replies.
  • AI in the workflow: When AI drafts replies or suggests content, someone still needs to review and approve it. Governed workflows keep AI output on-brand and on-policy.
  • Multiple brands or clients: Agencies and multi-market teams need separated permissions and reporting so one client’s assets never surface in another’s workspace.

The common thread: collaboration problems are rarely about effort. They’re about visibility.

What should you look for in a social media collaboration tool?

Look for a tool that handles communication, approvals, planning, and reporting in one place. Those four capabilities cover the moments where handoffs usually stall, so they’re the fastest way to narrow a shortlist.

Team communication and real-time commenting

A good social media collaboration tool should streamline team communication. Collaboration features like task assignments, approval tracking, and real-time commenting make this possible.

One of the biggest mistakes teams make is adding more tools to the toolbox. Suddenly, strategy lives in one platform, drafts in another, feedback in email, and quick questions in Slack.

This can easily create bottlenecks. You’re switching tabs, digging through threads, and trying to piece together context from scattered conversations.

To avoid the chaos, look for collaboration tools that centralize communication.

For example, in Hootsuite Social OS, Nest gives teams one unified inbox where they can assign conversations, hand off customer service inquiries, and see full message history in one view. Wisdom sits alongside it, so anyone on the team can ask questions about performance or workload without opening a separate reporting tool.

Real-time commenting also allows teams to collaborate on drafts and engagement without leaving the workflow.

Approval workflows and role-based permissions

Approvals are where most social workflows slow down, so this is worth checking carefully during a demo. Look for multi-step approval routing, clear draft statuses, and role-based permissions that define who can create, edit, approve, and publish.

Automation helps here too. Saved replies, automatic approval routing, and task triggers reduce repetitive work, which gives teams more time to collaborate on creative assignments or focus on strategy.

What is the value of social media for a business? 

Social media creates value by helping a business stay visible, relevant, and connected to the people it wants to reach.

Social media value is the full impact social media has on your business. Social media ROI is more specific: it’s the financial return you get compared to what you spent.

articles.title: Patrick Dempsey Is the New Face of Guardant Health’s ‘The Reckoning’ Campaign
articles.fullContent:
By Andrea Michelson Patrick Dempsey, best known for playing neurosurgeon Dr. Derek Shepherd in Grey’s Anatomy, is shifting focus to general oncology in a new ad campaign by Guardant Health urging Americans to get screened early for colorectal cancer.

The campaign, titled “The Reckoning,” features a somber tribute video memorializing those who have died of colorectal cancer in recent years and states that 55,000 more Americans will lose their lives to colorectal cancer this year. This is Guardant’s first campaign of such a scale: a national, multi-million dollar effort that is running across major cable, streaming, and digital platforms as of Monday.

In the ad spot, Dempsey faces a wall of names and ages of people who have died of colorectal cancer, some as young as 49. The actor and cancer advocate goes on to explain that getting screened for colorectal cancer from the age of 45 onwards can change the prognosis, as these cancers are significantly more treatable if caught early.

Colorectal cancer is now the second-leading cause of cancer death in the US, making this moment “a critical inflection point” for screening with Shield™, Steve Murphy, vp of marketing at Guardant Health told ADWEEK.

“Despite decades of access to other screening tests, more than 54 million Americans remain overdue for screening,” Murphy wrote in an email to ADWEEK. “What’s more, colorectal cancer rates are rising among younger adults and it is now the leading cause of cancer death for those under 50.”

Guardant introduced Shield™, a blood test for colorectal cancer detection, in 2022. For a medical specialty that usually requires a colonoscopy to screen for cancer, the development was revolutionary.

In 2024, the Food and Drug Administration officially approved Shield™ as the first blood test to qualify as a primary screening option for colorectal cancer. More recently, the American Cancer Society updated its colorectal cancer screening guidelines to include the Shield™ blood test, Murphy told ADWEEK.

Now the leading blood test for colorectal cancer detection, Shield™ is “helping to remove the barriers that have historically kept people from getting screened,” Murphy added.

Guardant first announced its partnership with Dempsey in March , sharing a video of the actor getting screened with Shield™ across digital channels.  Dempsey’s cancer advocacy dates back to 2008, when he founded the Dempsey Center, a holistic care center for people impacted by cancer. At the time, his mother was battling ovarian cancer. She died of the illness in 2014.  Since then, Dempsey has continued to raise awareness for cancer research and screenings, and he was even named one of the 100 Most Influential People in Oncology by OncoDaily last year.

The actor’s experience helped shape the Guardant campaign, Murphy said, emphasizing a twofold mission of encouraging people to get screened for colorectal cancer while honoring those who have died of the disease.

“Together, we wanted the campaign to reflect the real human impact of cancer and make sure the people and families behind the statistics remained at the center of the story,” Murphy told ADWEEK.

Andrea Michelson is the healthcare marketing reporter at ADWEEK. She previously covered the coronavirus pandemic for Business Insider and was part of the New York Times Covid mapping effort in 2020.

articles.title: How to build a social media team in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. High-performing social media teams include strategy, content, community, analytics, and paid roles scaled to your organization’s needs.
  2. Social teams connect daily execution to broader business goals like brand awareness, customer experience, and revenue.
  3. Team structure matters as much as who you hire—hub-and-spoke, center of excellence, and functional models serve different organizational needs.
  4. Building the right team depends on your budget, goals, and skill gaps.
  5. AI is reshaping social media teams in 2026 by shifting what each role focuses on and how teams collaborate.

What is a social media team?

A social media team is responsible for planning, creating, publishing, and managing a brand’s social media presence.

A typical social media team includes:

  • Strategists: Set goals and define content direction
  • Content creators: Write posts and create visuals or videos
  • Community managers: Respond to comments and direct messages (DMs)
  • Analysts: Track performance and optimize strategy
  • Social media managers: Oversee planning, publishing, and day-to-day execution across social media channels
  • Paid social specialists: Manage ad campaigns and budgets
  • Influencer managers: Handle creator collaborations and campaigns

Not every social media team looks the same. For example, a small business might have one or two people wearing multiple hats, while larger organizations have dedicated specialists for each role.

At the same time, some roles might be handled in-house, while others may be outsourced to freelancers or agencies, depending on the team’s size, budget, and needs.

The size and makeup of the team depend on the organization’s maturity. Startups often begin with a single social media manager who handles both strategy and execution, while organizations with established programs add specialists as volume, channels, and compliance requirements grow.

AI has changed the math here too. With AI-assisted drafting, tagging, and reporting, a smaller team can cover more ground, which makes the question less about headcount alone and more about which skills you genuinely need in-house. In short: A social media team is the group that owns your brand’s presence on social, sized and structured around your goals rather than a fixed template.

Bonus: Our free social media manager career toolkit includes resume, cover letter, and portfolio templates, along with a complete guide to social media job descriptions and frequently asked interview questions. You got this!

What does a social media team do?

A social media team is responsible for everything from daily posting to long-term strategy.

That means:

  • Managing a content calendar
  • Creating posts, videos, and visuals
  • Scheduling and publishing social media posts
  • Engaging with followers through comments and DMs
  • Monitoring trends, mentions, and conversations
  • Tracking performance and optimizing future content

But it’s not just execution. A strong social team connects social media to real business goals, whether that’s brand awareness, customer support, or sales.

At larger organizations, the remit stretches well beyond publishing. Social teams often own strategic functions that other departments depend on:

  • Social listening: Feeding customer feedback and competitor intelligence to product and marketing teams
  • Crisis management: Monitoring for risks and managing the brand’s response during sensitive events
  • Social selling: Partnering with sales teams to identify and engage prospects
  • Employee advocacy: Training and empowering employees to share brand content on their own profiles

In essence, the team handles the daily work of publishing and engagement while also feeding intelligence, risk signals, and revenue opportunities back into the wider business.

Social media team structures to consider

Before you decide who to hire, it helps to decide how the team will be organized. Your social media team structure shapes who owns strategy, how quickly content ships, and how consistent your brand looks across markets.

Here are four common models and where each one fits best.

Functional structure

In a functional structure, the team is organized by skill: content, community, analytics, and paid social each have a clear owner.

This works well for mid-size organizations with a dedicated social team and a single brand. The upside is clear ownership and deep expertise in each area. The tradeoff is that specialists can drift into silos, so someone needs to connect the work back to a single strategy.

Hub-and-spoke structure

A hub-and-spoke model puts a central team in charge of strategy, brand voice, and standards, while regional or business-unit teams handle local execution.

It’s a strong fit for multi-brand or multi-region enterprises that need global consistency and local relevance at the same time. The main cost is coordination: without shared calendars, approval workflows, and clear guardrails, the spokes drift.

Center of excellence

  • A high-converting landing page drives one specific action. Every element on the page should serve that single goal.
  • The median landing page converts at 6.6 percent across all industries. Your target should reflect your vertical, since averages range from under 2 percent in ecommerce to over 10 percent in other industries.

  • High-converting landing pages follow six core formats: text-only, lead generation, click-through, long-form, video, and SEO. Each format serves different goals, so choose yours based on the action you want visitors to take.

Ever wondered why your landing page pulls in traffic but barely converts anyone?

You’re not alone. 

The median landing page converts about 6.6 percent of visitors, and plenty of pages fall well below that. 

The problem is rarely traffic or budget. It’s the page.

Effective landing pages follow a proven structure, with every element earning its place through testing. I’ll walk you through how that process works so you can stop guessing and start optimizing with a clear plan.

What Is a High-Converting Landing Page?

A high-converting landing page is a webpage that excels at getting visitors to take one specific action. That could be signing up for a newsletter, registering for a webinar, claiming a discount, making a purchase, or downloading your app. 

Here’s an example from Revolut that directs visitors to download the digital banking company’s app: 

A strong landing page turns visitors into new subscribers and fresh leads, which you can nurture through your sales funnel until they’re ready to buy.

Core elements include a compelling call to action (CTA), a sign-up form, an attention-grabbing headline, and subheadings. It also contains easy-to-read content, images, and perhaps a video.

High-priority elements like your sign-up form should go above the fold (the visible part of the webpage when you first see it) for maximum visibility. I’ll cover placement strategy in more detail later. 

Types of High-Converting Landing Pages

High-converting landing pages come in several formats. Here are the ones worth knowing about.

Text-Only Landing Pages

These skip the videos and heavy graphics, relying on copy and a few supporting images to keep the focus on the message.

Copyblogger is a strong example that pairs minimal visuals with a clear CTA button.

Lead Generation Landing Pages

Lead generation landing pages collect details such as a name, email, and phone number. The idea is to turn prospects into leads by offering a free lead magnet, such as templates, a short course, eBooks, or access to a webinar.

This is how Workhuman uses them:

Although the form is relatively extensive (with several additional fields out of view), it makes segmenting and targeting easier. Its basic but striking design keeps it clutter-free while relaying the essential information.

Click-Through Landing Pages

Click-through landing page conversions aim to get people to take an action, such as signing up for a freebie, requesting a product demo, registering for an event, or buying a product. Typical features include a clear CTA, an engaging headline, and magnetic content designed to persuade the reader.

articles.title: How to measure social media with Google Analytics (GA4)
articles.fullContent:
Your native social media analytics show you how your brand is performing on social. But what happens outside of the platform? How do you track performance once the clicks turn into website traffic — and ultimately, conversions? This translates social media performance into business outcomes.

Yet according to the 2025 Impact of Social Media Marketing report, only 44% of leaders rate their social teams as experts in measuring business impact. Meanwhile, brands get a significant portion of their traffic from social. To be specific, social media accounts for 10.12% of global traffic. The number rises to 15.23% for socially driven markets like the United States.

Tracking social media traffic gives you a comprehensive picture of how social drives your broader business goals. And Google Analytics (GA4) offers a robust solution for tracking social media performance once it leaves native platforms.

This post explores how to measure social media with Google Analytics and gain more in-depth performance insights. Let’s get started.

Why measure social media with Google Analytics?

Google Analytics enables you to measure your social metrics holistically, adding context to your social media reports by aligning with your broader marketing goals. Specifically, it delivers value in two crucial ways:

Connect social to business goals

Social metrics don’t live in a vacuum. They need to be aligned to the broader marketing efforts and org-wide business goals.

Connecting Google Analytics and social media ties social media performance to business goals. This is vital because 65% of marketing leaders in the 2025 Sprout Social Index ™ say this is the top way to secure social investment.

For example, Google Analytics for social media will tell you how visitors coming from specific platforms are interacting with your content. You can compare the key performance indicators between different traffic sources to see how social ultimately drives engaged visitors.

Google Analytics captures funnel metrics such as goal completions and identifies where conversion discrepancies occur. This ensures your top-funnel and mid-funnel efforts are in sync. Together, these efforts prove your social media return on investment (ROI) and show the impact on business growth.

Understand your audience

Social metrics from Google Analytics track audience behavior, interests and where they spend their time on your site. As you gain a better understanding of your audience, you have the insights to craft compelling content and social tactics that resonate.

How GA4 sorts your social traffic: Organic social vs. paid social

Social media tracking in Google Analytics is available for both organic and paid social. For organic social, Google Analytics will track a recognized social source or an accepted utm_medium. Meanwhile, paid social needs a paid medium.

Here’s how GA4 sorts the traffic coming from social:

Tag your social links with UTM parameters

UTM parameters allow you to tag your social links, so you can tie traffic to specific campaigns and posts. The link can consist of various parameters like:

  • utm_source: Identifies the specific platform, like facebook or linkedin.
  • utm_medium: Identifies the marketing channel type, such as social or paid-social.
  • utm_campaign: Identifies a specific product launch, promo or seasonal push, like summer_sale.
  • utm_content: Distinguishes specific links or creative variations within the same post, like image or video

Say you want to track traffic coming from Facebook for your spring collection launch. Your promo post could have the following tag:

https://www.example.com/spring-collection?utm_source=facebook&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=spring_launch

But UTM tracking for social involves keeping track of every link for multiple posts, platforms and campaigns. This quickly becomes messy and confusing, especially for time-strapped solo marketers.

Sprout Social’s Bitly integration streamlines this process, letting you shorten UTM links in one click while creating a new post. It’s easier to track and manage your links without pulling up a separate spreadsheet.

4 social media insights to track in Google Analytics

To get the most out of Google Analytics for social media, you need to pay attention to the metrics that will connect social to business performance. These data points prove how your social strategy is driving website traffic. You’ll demonstrate how your social media efforts deliver ROI beyond the vanity metrics.

Here are the key social media metrics to track with GA4:

Category Metric What it shows Why it matters Audience Demographics Location, age and language of social visitors Confirms if your social content attracts your target buyer persona. Acquisition Session source/medium Specific platform (e.g., facebook/referral) or campaign driving traffic Identifies which exact social network or post delivers the highest volume of visitors. Web Engagement Sessions and Engaged Sessions Visits that last longer than 10 seconds, feature a conversion, or view 2+ pages. Filters out accidental clicks to show real interest from social traffic. Web Engagement Average Engagement Time The average length of time a user actively spends on your site. Measures if the content on your site matches the promise of your social post.

Measure social media conversions and ROI in GA4

Whether you want people to sign up for a demo or buy your products, conversions accurately measure your social media ROI.

Google Analytics lets you measure the conversions resulting from your social media traffic through key events (formerly called conversions).

Conditions online can be harrowing. All of us are susceptible to doom-scrolling—absorbing the intensity of global political, humanitarian and climate crises with the flick of a thumb. Not to mention comparing our lives to influencers’ glossy content or our acquaintances’ highlight reels, letting unhealthy comparisons rear their ugly head.

With such dark sides to social, lawmakers worldwide have started to wonder: Do they have a responsibility to enact social media bans that protect children? Consumers think so, with 68% saying they support such bans, according to Sprout Social’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey. Those with young children are the most likely to rally behind them.

For social media marketers, who already face a number of internal and external challenges in the course of doing their jobs, this means even more stress and brand safety risks. Many countries have already implemented, passed or strongly considered a social media ban. And Meta’s landmark youth safety settlement means a new series of safeguards will be required on Instagram and Facebook, with a call for more networks to follow suit.

This new legislation may make it more difficult to reach certain audiences, publish content efficiently, and stay compliant with ever-changing rule books and country-specific laws. Zooming out, as the world’s economies become more connected, it’s going to prove challenging for global brands to comply with so many disparate policies and maintain relevance.

To make it easier to navigate, we’ve laid out the facts we have so far about current and proposed social media bans. We’ve also asked global marketers for their takes on how social teams should adjust their workflows and content strategies as regulations around social media become more common.

Networks are regulating in response to public concern and settlements

Social media networks are responding to proposed legislation and judicial decisions by updating their functionality and adding safeguards, like parental controls, for youth safety.

In lockstep with consumer preferences, many major platforms now give parents more control over their children’s experience online.

Networks like Meta, Snapchat, WhatsApp and YouTube are tightening parental controls, designing family-friendly app experiences, enforcing time limits and restricting sensitive content to improve the social media experience for younger generations. They’re also giving parents a broader window into what kids are doing online–offering ways to manage child privacy settings, supervise activity and limit conversations with AI chatbots.

The overarching impact of the Meta youth safety settlement

While networks have slowly started to self-regulate, the latest Meta youth safety settlement has fast tracked several changes to pay attention to.

Through the terms of the settlement, Meta has agreed to enforce the following restrictions to make their platforms safer for kids:

  • Two-hour daily time limit
  • Turning off nighttime access to their apps
  • No notifications during school hours to limit interruptions during critical learning periods
  • Prompts that interrupt teens after 15 minutes of continuous screen time to lessen mindless scrolling
  • More parental controls to empower parents to design the experience they want for their children

These terms cement changes that will likely extend beyond Instagram and Facebook, too, with part of Meta’s payout depending on TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat adopting similar rules.

It’s also worth noting, this settlement sets a precedent: constraints on reaching minors are arriving faster through settlements than through official legislation.

How brands can adjust to social media restrictions

Even if you aren’t operating within the jurisdiction of a legislative social media ban, the incoming changes based on the Meta settlement begs the question: what does this mean for brands?

First and foremost, it’s critical to understand how these changes will impact your brand (if at all). Changes to your brand’s strategy and overall marketing tactics should be minimal since these new safeguards benefit youth demographics that brands don’t market to.

But, there are a few downstream impacts to understand:

Instead, shift focus to look at stronger engagement and conversion metrics to understand what’s happening with the people who actually have buying power.

articles.fullContent:
Brand loyalty has always been hard to win. Today, it’s even easier to lose.

Consumers increasingly encounter brands across social networks, creator communities and other digital spaces businesses don’t control. At the same time, the rise of AI-generated content and misinformation has made people more skeptical about what they see online.

Customer sentiment can shift quickly in this environment, so brands need to understand what people are saying while those conversations still matter. Sales data, surveys and quarterly reports reveal useful patterns, but by the time teams use them, customers may already feel differently, or their loyalty is too far gone.

Building lasting brand loyalty depends on how quickly brands understand what audiences are saying, what’s driving those conversations and how to respond. Social intelligence gives teams a real-time view of what customers care about and how expectations are shifting.

In this guide, we’ll explore what brand loyalty really means, why it’s harder to earn and how brands can strengthen it.

What is brand loyalty? (And how it’s different from brand affinity)

What is brand loyalty?

Brand loyalty is a customer’s ongoing preference for one brand over its competitors, driven by trust and emotional connection rather than convenience or habit alone.

Brand loyalty is evident in what customers do: repeatedly choosing the same brand, recommending it to others or sticking with it when competitors offer a cheaper or more convenient option.

Brand affinity reflects what customers feel: a sense of connection to a brand based on shared values, identity or experiences.

The two often reinforce each other, but they aren’t interchangeable. The same goes for customer loyalty and brand awareness.

What it measures Example signal Brand loyalty A customer’s ongoing preference for a brand Repeatedly choosing the brand over competitors Brand affinity Engagement and emotional connection to a brand Feeling that the brand reflects your values or identity Customer loyalty Repeat behavior based on the overall customer relationship Continuing to buy because of service, rewards or convenience Brand awareness Familiarity with or recognition of a brand Recognizing the brand name, logo or products

Think of brand loyalty like a lasting friendship. One good conversation rarely creates a close relationship. Trust builds through repeated experiences that show someone is reliable and understands what matters to you.

Brands earn loyalty in much the same way. Each positive interaction gives customers another reason to return, while repeated missteps chip away at loyalty over time.

Why brand loyalty is harder to earn

Brand loyalty now competes with a much wider range of influences. A customer might discover a product through a creator, read mixed reviews on Reddit and see a critical TikTok about the company before they ever visit the brand’s website. By then, they’ve already formed an impression.

People are also approaching online content with more skepticism. According to Sprout’s Q1 2026 Pulse Survey, 35% of social users say their trust in social content has decreased over the past year. Misinformation was the most common reason, cited by 30% of respondents. Another 20% pointed to unregulated AI content. And 88% agree AI video tools have reduced their trust in the news they see on social.

Brand interactions face the same scrutiny. An overly polished testimonial might feel less credible if customers suspect AI involvement. A vague response to criticism can fuel more questions. A creator partnership can also backfire if the recommendation feels inauthentic or the sponsorship isn’t transparent.

The trust bar is higher now. Customers are paying closer attention to whether a company’s actions match what it says. Loyalty increasingly depends on the credibility brands build through every interaction, including those outside their own channels.

Why is brand loyalty important?

Brand loyalty gives businesses more stability in a crowded market. Loyal customers are more likely to keep choosing a brand even when competitors enter the picture, supporting several business outcomes:

  • Protect revenue: Loyal customers are less likely to churn. For example, a software company with strong loyalty may retain more subscribers after a competitor launches a lower-priced plan.
  • Lower acquisition pressure: A strong base of repeat customers reduces the need to replace every lost customer through paid acquisition.
  • Drive organic growth: Loyal customers often recommend brands through reviews, referrals and social conversation. A recommendation in a niche community can influence new buyers without the brand having to initiate it.
  • Strengthen business planning: Consistent loyalty can make revenue more predictable and reveal what customers value. Repeated praise for a specific feature, for instance, gives product teams clearer direction on where to invest.

Taken together, loyalty becomes a brand health marker, not just a marketing KPI.

How brands miss the loyalty signal

Most brands aren’t short on customer data. The problem is often timing.

A complaint might surface on social days before it comes up in a customer survey. Customers might start expecting a feature your competitor just launched before sales data reflects the shift. By the time the right team gets the information, the best window to respond may have passed.

Sprout’s Social Intelligence Report found that 86% of professionals say they’ve missed opportunities in the past two years because consumer insights were delayed, siloed or underused. Reacting too slowly to a market shift was the most common missed opportunity, cited by 33% of respondents. And only 10% of organizations say they can act on a social insight within hours.

How teams capture and organize customer data contributes to the gap. Different systems capture different parts of the customer picture:

  • Business intelligence (BI) looks backward at business performance, including sales and revenue.
  • Customer intelligence (CI) captures current and past customer profiles and purchase history, often through CRM and transaction data.
  • Social intelligence adds human context by revealing what people are saying and how they feel right now.

Disconnected data makes it harder for teams to respond at the right moment. According to Sprout’s Q4 2025 Pulse Survey, 55% of consumers say brands do a good job listening but don’t always act on what they hear. Only 31% say brands do both well.

For loyalty, listening alone isn’t enough. Connecting real-time audience signals with other customer data gives teams the full picture and a chance to address problems before frustration turns into churn.

How to build brand loyalty that lasts

  • The global education sector is expected to reach $10 trillion in value by 2030, making digital marketing essential for standing out in this competitive industry.
  • Digital marketing in higher education means reaching four distinct audiences (students, parents, counselors, and B2B tech buyers) with messaging tailored to what they actually care about.
  • Education marketing requires a unique approach due to trust-building, long decision cycles, and diverse audiences.
  • Proven strategies like local SEO, paid advertising, and social media engagement can drive enrollment and engagement.
  • The right tools, data-driven insights, and experienced agency support drive sustainable growth and measurable return on investment (ROI).

The global education sector is set to reach $10 trillion in value by 2030, powered by growth in developing markets as well as education technology reaching new heights. Both of those factors add up to a lot of competition out there for your education business or clients.

Compounding that is the fact that the way students and parents search for schools has changed. With a growing online audience and competition from all angles, institutions need to stand out, and digital marketing is how they’ll do it.

In this guide, we’re diving deep into the strategies that work, the challenges and common mistakes you might face, and how to conquer them like a pro. 

What Is Education Marketing?

Digital marketing for education encompasses the strategies and tools used by schools, universities, edtech companies, training centers, and any other business in the niche to promote their offerings online. It’s a multifaceted approach that includes:

  • Search engine optimization (SEO) for visibility: Building a well-optimized site puts your institution at the top of search results for relevant queries. 
  • Pay-per-click (PPC) campaigns: Buying PPC campaigns enables you to focus on more targeted traffic on conventional search engines like Google and Bing, social media, connected TV devices, or even in apps.
  • Social media engagement: Building meaningful connections with audiences on popular social media platforms gives you a chance to both improve your perception and draw in potential leads.
  • Content marketing: Creating value-driven content, such as blogs and videos, that address your audience’s pain points.

Why Digital Marketing Matters for Education

The education sector’s target audience (students, parents, and professionals) turns to the web to research options before making decisions. One study showed that when looking into higher education opportunities, 63 percent of students start their research on traditional search engines, and 60 percent used popular social media platforms. 

This applies across education, though. A school district shopping for software and new parents shopping for a daycare will both start online.

Digital marketing simplifies this process by delivering the right information at the right time. Educational institutions that invest in digital marketing can:

  • Build brand authority: A consistent online reputation helps establish your business as a trustworthy and reliable option. 
  • Enhance engagement: Digital marketing campaigns help your team connect with audiences where they are through meaningful and interactive content.
  • Boost conversions: Data-driven campaigns showing the value of your offerings will help convert inquiries into enrollments.

An effective digital campaign ensures that your business stays top of mind with your target audience, showing what you do best and moving them to a conversion.

What Makes Education Marketing Different

Marketing in the education sector presents unique challenges and opportunities. Here’s what sets it apart:

  1. Building Trust: Prospective students and parents alike are going to be concerned about the quality and credibility of institutions. The same applies to education technology (edtech) or other branches of the industry. Trust-building will be essential given the substantial investments in education.
  2. Long Decision Cycles: Customer decisions often involve months of research and multiple touchpoints. You need to build campaigns that can retain value during the entire cycle.
  3. Localized Marketing: An education marketing strategy tailored to the community where a specific school or business operates will perform much better than a broad, one-size-fits-all approach.
  4. Storytelling: A student’s educational experience is often an emotional journey for them, as well as their parents and teachers. Painting the picture of the role your school or business plays in that journey is critical for business conversions.
  5. Complex Stakeholders: Education marketing has to cater to students, parents, sponsors, and counselors simultaneously. Building out segments and personalized campaigns for each group is key to success.

Education Marketing Channels

No single channel carries an entire education marketing program on its own. The schools and edtech brands seeing the strongest results run a mix, meeting different audiences at different points in a decision cycle that can stretch on for months.

Below, I’ve broken down the four channels that consistently drive results in marketing for education. Each plays a specific role, and the smartest programs coordinate them to account for each customer’s unique buyer journey.

SEO and Local Search

Local SEO matters more in education than in most industries because most students and parents are searching for schools or programs nearby. That means researching location-based keywords and showing up in local search results is disproportionately important to your education marketing strategy compared to other channels.

Start by optimizing your education website for location-based keywords, like “top private schools in [city].”

The air is getting crisp, pumpkin spice-flavored treats are returning to store shelves and scary movies are back in rotation. Autumn is a fan favorite, and the season’s star holiday, Halloween, is growing in popularity amongst all ages. In the US alone, 73% of people participate in the holiday in some way. For brands, Halloween is a great chance to get in on the spooky fun with creative themed content.

The key to scaring up successful seasonal content: Halloween posts live or die by discoverability, not just cute captions.

Hashtags are only one piece of the formula. They don’t work quite the same as they used to; hashtagging is no longer a content reach shortcut, but instead a useful content signal. Social media algorithms use hashtags to categorize and distribute your content to the right audiences.

Keep reading (if you dare) to uncover trending Halloween hashtags and content ideas to put in your arsenal.

10 best all-purpose Halloween hashtags

If you need a quick list to start, these 10 hashtags have good popularity and cover a variety of topics. Depending on your brand and audience, you can use these to focus on a range of products, services, ideas and themes.

  1. #Halloween or #Halloween2026
  2. #HalloweenCostume
  3. #Autumn or #Fall
  4. #HappyHalloween
  5. #SpookySeason or #SpookySzn
  6. #October
  7. #HalloweenDecor
  8. #HalloweenVibes
  9. #HalloweenHaul
  10. #PumpkinSpice

How to choose the right hashtags for Halloween

Most of us enjoy a mix of candy in our Trick-or-Treat bags, and algorithms appreciate variety in your content tagging, too. To get the most traction, go for a selection of Halloween-centric hashtags that span broad discussions, niche topics and branded hashtags where appropriate.

For example, #horror and #HorrorMovies are major hashtags that pop up around movies, TV shows and seasonal attractions this time of year. Depending on your brand’s offerings, you could use this hashtag alongside niche ones like #HorrorManga, #HorrorFiction or #HorrorBooks to target more specific audience segments.

If your brand ties directly to the horror entertainment scene, you could also create a branded hashtag to match, like streaming platform Shudder did with their #ShudderSundays tag. You can even jump on a hashtag holiday like #NationalHorrorMovieDay on October 23rd. Burger chain A&W got in on the fun with horror movie posters featuring their menu items and mascots.

Social media lives on culture, so try to capitalize on Halloween pop culture trends when selecting your hashtag line up. It’s what your audience expects, with 93% of consumers thinking it’s important for brands to keep up with online culture. This includes new horror movies, classic Halloween characters (like #MichaelMyers or #FreddyKrueger) and trending shows or memes that speak to your audience’s interests.

Once you’ve curated your selection of hashtags for the season, make sure to follow best practices for adding them in. This can vary by network. On Instagram and TikTok, the algorithm currently favors hashtags within captions versus the first comment. Place a few strategic hashtags at the end of your caption. On Facebook, you can work hashtags directly into sentences in the post itself. Hashtags don’t provide discoverability value in your social media bios, but placing branded hashtags here can let your audience know they exist.

Halloween hashtags for every category

There are so many ways to get in on spooky celebrations via hashtags, from food to decor to scene-setting aesthetics. We’ve put together ideas across categories to give you a bank to pull from no matter how your brand plans to participate.

General Halloween hashtags

In addition to the all-purpose hashtags listed above, you can riff on them to tap into more specific Halloween conversations. You can also choose hashtags for specific concepts like ghosts and goblins. There are additional days of significance around Halloween, both modern and traditional, that also have hashtags you can apply if they’re a fit for your brand.

articles.title: Real Estate Marketing: A Complete Guide for 2026
articles.fullContent:
If you’re running marketing for a real estate brand, you already know the deal. Zillow, Realtor.com, and Redfin sit at the top of nearly every high-volume query, and AI Overviews are quietly compressing what’s left of the informational clicks below. That’s the real estate marketing challenge in 2026. Everyone else has already adopted the basics, so pulling ahead now takes a creative, targeted strategy.

This guide walks through a five-step framework for building a real estate marketing plan. From there, you’ll get a breakdown of how AI search and portal competition are reshaping the search engine results pages (SERPs), plus a client case study showing what real growth looks like when the strategy lands.

You’ll finish this guide with a clear picture of what to do next for your real estate marketing strategy in 2026.

Key Takeaways

  • Zillow, Realtor.com, and Redfin dominate head-term SERPs, so marketing wins come from targeting long-tail and hyperlocal queries the portals ignore. 
  • Google’s AI Overviews are causing people to click less. Structure content for AI citation and reinforce E-E-A-T signals to stay visible. 
  • A five-step marketing plan (ICPs, brand identity, website, omnichannel, offline) is the foundation. Skip a step and everything downstream weakens. 
  • Owned channels like email and direct mail are how “the little guy” can fight against the real estate giants by routing buyers around third-party portals. 
  • NP Digital used the tactics in this guide to stack significant wins for our client, Homeway Real Estate.

What Is Real Estate Marketing?

Real estate marketing is the practice of promoting properties available for sale or rent. It takes the Four Ps of marketing (Product, Price, Place, and Promotion) and adapts them to the real estate market. 

The marketing plan is important because of the hyper-competitive nature of the real estate industry. A proper strategy could give you a powerful competitive edge. 

Here are the three main benefits of marketing for real estate professionals: 

  • Builds trust with the customer base: A consistent presence assures potential buyers that they’re dealing with the right person to help them find their dream property. 
  • Makes the brand more memorable: A recognizable brand increases the chances that buyers will seek the brand out when they enter the market. 
  • Enables more efficient selling: A long-term marketing strategy provides established channels to quickly promote new properties when they become available, cutting down on promotion and admin costs. 

National Association of Realtors (NAR) data tells us that every buyer uses the internet at some point during their home search, and 46 percent take their first step online (versus 20 percent who start by contacting an agent). The marketing strategy used could be the difference between a brokerage that compounds visibility for years and one that keeps starting from zero on every new listing.

How to Build a Real Estate Marketing Plan

You can develop a solid real estate marketing management plan in five simple steps. The order matters because each step sets up the next, so don’t skip anything. It usually means going back to fix something later.

We’ll start with the most important step of any marketing plan: defining who you’re trying to reach. From there, we’ll discuss your brand’s presence and finish with the optimal digital strategy, as well as offline channels you can use to supplement it. 

Here’s how the framework breaks down.

1. Define Your Ideal Customer Profiles (ICPs)

What type of people would make ideal sellers or renters?

Even if you understand your ideal customer, it’s important to map them out clearly on paper. These definitions will form the basis of the real estate marketing plan you implement, so ICPs could always use more fine-tuning. The more detailed, the better.

Most agents typically target several distinct ICPs that cover a whole portfolio of properties. 

Here are three example ICPs: 

  • Three to four-person families with a joint annual income of $150,000 looking to purchase suburban detached or semi-detached houses.
  • Young professionals with high disposable income searching for inner-city apartments to rent in the $2000 to $3000/month price range with an active local nightlife nearby.
  • Retirees with a budget of $300,000 to $500,000 in the market for semi-rural properties with good car access to local amenities like hospitals, supermarkets, and shops.

Research the following attributes when putting together your customer profiles:

  • Budget for rent or purchase
  • Desired location and property type
  • Specific property features (garage, bathrooms, garden)
  • Timeline (weeks or months)
  • Required nearby amenities (schools, transport, roads, etc.)

Treat these definitions as segmentation blocks you can plan against. Each ICP needs its own creative and channel mix. It also makes sense to give each segment its own definition of a win.

Take the three examples above. The suburban family segment probably converts best on Facebook and YouTube with school-district and neighborhood-tour content, and you might measure campaign success on booked showings per dollar. The young-professional rental segment leans on Instagram Reels and TikTok walkthroughs of the units and the neighborhood, with success measured by rental applications submitted. Retirees might respond better to a Google search or a referral-driven email, and success there could be measured by the number of in-person consultations booked.

You spent time crafting what you thought was a great meta description for your page. You agonized over word choice and character count for what felt like hours, only to have Google ignore it and choose a random sentence from your content to display as the search snippet. 

Why?

The short answer is that Google rewrites roughly 70 percent of meta descriptions. A stat like that may have you wondering if it’s even worth writing them on your own.

It is. The 30 percent of descriptions that Google doesn’t rewrite are your best shot at controlling your first impression in search. My team and I have also discovered that the surviving descriptions share a few common traits.

This guide covers those traits, or meta description best practices. I’ll show you what can earn you clicks in 2026, backed by real examples from brands doing it well. By the end, you’ll have a framework you can take to your business immediately.

What Is a Meta Description?

A meta description is a short HTML tag that summarizes the page’s content.

Readers can’t see meta descriptions or title tags for SEO without inspecting the code.

This meta tag’s importance shows up in the snippet on the search engine results page, below the page URL and title.  

Its job: to show readers what the page offers and persuade them to click. That’s why people often call it a page’s elevator pitch.

Are Meta Descriptions a Ranking Factor?

The short answer is no. Meta descriptions aren’t a direct ranking factor, and Google has confirmed this explicitly through its search advocate, John Mueller, as well as its own search documentation.

However, many SEOs believe that following meta description best practices can indirectly improve rankings. This is based on the assumptions that:

  • Compelling meta descriptions improve click-through rates (CTRs).
  • CTRs are a user signal that Google considers when ranking pages. More people clicking on your page signals to Google that it satisfies their search intent.
  • Well-written meta descriptions improve the user experience. They show readers what they can find on the page and help them decide if they want to visit it. If they do, they’re less likely to bounce, and bounce rates are a quality signal for Google.

That all sounds logical, but no recent large-scale studies confirm the positive impact of meta descriptions on CTR or traffic. Experiments conducted by SEOTesting indicated that optimizing meta descriptions had little effect on traffic, and a case study by SearchPilot showed that removing them improved CTRs.

So why write them at all? 

When Google does use your description, a well-written one that follows meta description best practices for SEO gives you real control over your snippet. Google will use your description when it “describes your page better than other parts of the content.”

A strong meta description can also influence how your page appears on social media. Platforms like Facebook and LinkedIn use a protocol called Open Graph (OG) tags to pull in a page’s title, description, and preview image when someone shares a link.

As social media users spread their attention across multiple platforms, more brands are expanding their presence to meet them there. According to our 2026 Social Media Content Strategy report, 87% of marketers plan to show up on more networks this year.

Cross-posting on social media is an excellent strategy for reaching new audiences, but it can also multiply your team’s workload, especially if you’re tailoring content to each platform.

This guide explains what cross-posting is, when it works (or backfires) and what each platform’s native rules allow. You’ll also learn how to cross-post easily with the Sprout Social Essentials plan.

What is cross-posting on social media?

Cross-posting means publishing the same content to two or more social media networks, either simultaneously or on a network-specific schedule.

But your posts shouldn’t be identical across platforms. A good cross-posting strategy preserves the core message or creative concept while optimizing the size, caption, format, tags, media and timing for each channel.

When you cross-post on social media effectively, you get content on your brand accounts quickly, freeing up your team for more strategic tasks like planning and engaging.

The right tools simplify the process. Sprout Social Essentials lets you cross-post to up to five social profiles at once. Use the unified Compose window to customize your post’s text, media and timing for each platform—no switching tabs.

Cross-posting vs. reposting vs. repurposing vs. sharing

Cross-posting, reposting, repurposing and sharing all extend the reach of your social content, but they describe different actions.

  • Cross-posting is when you publish your own content to several networks you control, with or without channel-specific editing.
  • Reposting is when you republish an existing post, yours or someone else’s, in its original form and usually within the same network.
  • Repurposing is when you rebuild an asset into one or several new formats to extend its life, increase reach and maximize ROI.
  • Sharing is when you distribute someone else’s post, either on your feed or to someone’s private inbox, through a native sharing button.

Here’s a quick table with examples of each term:

Term What it means Example Cross-posting Publishing one core post across multiple networks at the same time (or on an automated schedule) Publishing a ‘New Arrivals’ post on Instagram, LinkedIn and Facebook Reposting Resurfacing an existing post, yours or someone else’s, usually within the same network Reposting a customer’s Instagram post on your brand profile Repurposing Turning one asset into several different formats or deliverables Converting a webinar into three Reels and a LinkedIn carousel Sharing Distributing someone else’s post through a native sharing button Sharing a partner’s post to your feed or sending it through a direct message

Should you post the same content on every network?

Only cross-post content to networks where the topic is relevant and the format makes sense. Even then, “same content” should mean the same idea, not an untouched copy of the same post.

Exact duplication works for simple, time-sensitive updates. But for most campaigns, small changes to the hook, caption, tags, call-to-action, media and publish time give the post a better chance of meeting each audience’s expectations.

When cross-posting works well

Cross-posting works well when speed and consistency matter, or when audiences have similar needs across channels. Examples of content to cross-post include:

  • Company and product announcements: Launch dates, new locations, event registrations and important service updates benefit from a consistent message.
  • Evergreen education: Tips, how-to content, FAQs and research findings are useful across several networks, especially with minor tweaks.
  • Short-form video: A clean, watermark-free vertical video works across Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts.
  • Little to no audience overlap: If research shows your audience varies across platforms, cross-posting helps you reach more people without looking repetitive.

As for cadence, cross-post as often as the content fits each network, but balance it with platform-specific posts so every feed still feels original and worth following.

When to tailor or skip cross-posting

Create a separate post or stick to one network only when the content relies heavily on platform-specific behavior. Skip cross-posting in the following situations:

  • Format mismatch: A text-only update has no direct equivalent on TikTok, while a 10-minute landscape video won’t work on Instagram.
  • Overlapping audiences: Followers who see identical posts on several networks in quick succession will tune them out. Change the hook or stagger the timing.
  • Unique native features: Not every network supports features like polls, in-app sounds, stickers, live video, collaboration tools and document posts.
  • Varying audience expectations: Avoid cross-posting when content is built around platform-specific trends or needs a different angle, such as the business impact of an announcement on LinkedIn versus its human side on Instagram.

In these scenarios, the cons of cross-posting outweigh the pros. But that doesn’t mean cross-posting is bad for performance. Just avoid sharing identical or poorly adapted posts all the time as it makes your brand look repetitive and boring.

Benefits of cross-posting to multiple social channels

Market to different target demographics

Cross-posting helps your brand reach different customer groups without recreating content from scratch every single time.

Every network has its own mix of age groups, interests, professions and behaviors. For example, the latest social media demographics show that Facebook reaches 88% of Baby Boomers, compared with 39% for Instagram and 20% for TikTok.

articles.fullContent:
Known and beloved for its compelling short-form video content, TikTok has become a social powerhouse in Australia. According to The 2025 Sprout Social Index™, 39% of Australian social users turn to TikTok to keep up with trends in many areas, from finance to fashion, technology to travel. For businesses, this level of engagement represents a major marketing opportunity—but only if they know exactly how and why Australians are using the app.

The latest TikTok statistics in Australia point to an app whose role keeps shifting. What started as an entertainment feed now shapes how Australians discover products, research big decisions and connect with the brands they love. Marketers who understand that shift meet their audience where attention already lives and turn casual scrolling into real business results.

In this guide, we cover the most important TikTok statistics in Australia to help you build a smarter, data-led strategy. With these insights, you can guide your social strategy, spark TikTok campaign ideas and create content that truly resonates with Australian audiences.

Key TikTok statistics in Australia

TikTok is a major player in Australia’s social media landscape. As of late 2025, 10.9 million Australians aged 18 and over use the app, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report. These statistics show how deeply the network has embedded itself into everyday life:

  • More than 350,000 Australian businesses use TikTok, restated by the company in 2026.

  • Australian users spend an average of 1 hour 14 minutes a day in the app (August 2025), the highest daily figure of any social app in Australia, per DataReportal and We Are Social.

  • Per a Deloitte report, Australian TikTok users spend most of their time on the app watching videos, listening to audio and browsing feeds.

  • According to Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report, short-form videos (<60 seconds long) perform best on TikTok. Users are most interested in entertaining content, product discovery and influencer partnerships

With Sprout Social, you can schedule TikTok posts, track performance and spot emerging trends from the same platform you use to manage every other network.

The rise of TikTok in Australia: TikTok stats on growth in the Australian market

Although it’s been a major player in Australia’s social media landscape for years, TikTok is constantly evolving. What primarily began as an entertainment platform has transformed into a source of information, an outlet for cultural connection and a driver for social change.

  • In Q4 2024 alone, TikTok generated 186 million downloads from users globally.

  • TikTok ads reached 51.2% of Australian adults aged 18 and over at the end of 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • TikTok’s ad reach grew 13.9% year-on-year in Australia, adding 1.33 million users, the fastest growth of any major Australian platform, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Australia counted 21.0 million social media user identities in October 2025, equal to 77.7% of the population, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to a 2024 report from Oxford Economics, 19% of Australian users have donated to a charity or cause they saw on TikTok, and 18% have committed their time to volunteer.

TikTok Australia user and demographic statistics

TikTok appeals strongly to younger audiences; over 30% of its global audience is aged 18–24. Given that young people are Australia’s most active social shoppers, TikTok is an ideal platform for brands to connect with and sell to these users. From gender to income, here’s a more in-depth look at Australian TikTokers:

  • Around 74% of TikTok’s Australian user base is younger than 34, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • According to Statista, around 53.1% of Australians aged 18 and over use TikTok.

  • 72% of Gen Z have TikTok accounts, compared with 50% of users overall, per Sprout’s 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report.

  • Almost half (48%) of Australians aged 18 to 24 use TikTok to get news, per the University of Canberra’s Digital News Report 2026.

  • According to Statista, TikTok is more popular with Gen Z than other social networks.

  • TikTok’s adult advertising audience in Australia was 53.6% male and 46.4% female in late 2025, per DataReportal’s Digital 2026 Australia report.

  • Further, the 2026 Social Media Content Strategy Report reveals that 37% of Millennials globally have TikTok accounts.

  • A 2024 survey found that 41% of Gen Z shoppers had made purchases through social media in the past six months, followed closely by Millennials (40%).

  • Statista reports that, while Millennials favour Facebook for social shopping, Instagram and TikTok attract more Zoomers.

Australia’s social media ban for children under 16 reshapes this picture. It removes under-16s from the platform, which shifts TikTok’s Australian audience even further towards adults. Here’s what that means for your strategy.

How does Australia’s under-16 social media ban affect TikTok?

Australia’s under-16 social media ban took effect on 10 December 2025 under the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Bill 2024. It requires TikTok and nine other social media platforms to take reasonable steps to stop Australians under 16 from holding accounts, with fines of up to A$49.5 million for non-compliance, per the eSafety Commissioner.

Between all the DMs you need to answer and the posts you need to create, it’s time-consuming to maintain an active social media presence. And as you expand to more channels without increasing headcount, you get sucked into a productivity trap where you’re doing more work, but your results stagnate.

This is all too familiar for social media teams that do (almost) everything manually. The Social Media Productivity Report from Sprout Social even found that 63% of are unable to do high-impact work because they’re bogged down by manual tasks.

On the other hand, respondents who use dedicated tools to manage their social media are twice as likely to have enough time to get their work done.

This makes a strong case for marketers to start automating various aspects of their social media management. In this social media automation guide, we break down three essential steps to get started. Let’s take a look.

What social media automation means

Social media automation is the process of letting tools handle routine and repetitive tasks like scheduling posts or tracking brand mentions. This gives you back the time needed for more meaningful work that requires human input, whether that’s responding to your DMs or creating high-quality content.

Rather than “replacing you,” automation allows you to free up time by automating the routine. So you have more time to spend on personalizing the meaningful.

Step 1: Centralize your publishing

Connect your profiles to one dashboard

You waste time when you’re manually logging into different profiles to schedule every post individually. Streamline the process by connecting all your social media profiles to a centralized publishing dashboard.

A social media management platform like Sprout consolidates your publishing through a single dashboard. This lets you connect your profiles across different social networks and manage your publishing in one place. When you create a new post to schedule, all you have to do is select the profile(s) where you want to publish it.

Build a lightweight content calendar

Before all the automation comes the planning. And you need to plan your posts ahead of time before you can schedule them.

A content calendar makes it easy to do this and organize your publishing efforts. When you already have content planned for the entire week or month, you can quickly start creating posts without spending too much time on ideation.

And you don’t have to build an elaborate calendar, either. Keep it simple with a clear outline of the essentials:

  • Publishing date and time
  • Platform and profile
  • Content pillar or topic
  • Format

Sprout’s content calendar helps you visualize your planned posts across all your profiles. It lets you create and schedule posts directly within the calendar, which simplifies your publishing automation. You can even drag and drop posts to easily adjust your publishing cadence for optimal frequency.

Schedule around optimal send times

Effective publishing automation is highly strategic. It’s less about the publishing volume and more about the timing precision. When you schedule your posts to automatically go live, you need to time them to make sure they reach audiences when they’re most active.

Sprout’s social media automation features like Sprout Queue let you do just that. It automatically sends out your posts at a time of your choosing, so you no longer have to set reminders to remember when it’s time to post. You can schedule posts in bulk and for the entire month, freeing up time to focus on more high-impact tasks.

ViralPost™ takes the guesswork out of scheduling with optimal send time recommendations. It analyzes your audience and their engagement patterns to figure out when to deliver content for the greatest impact.

Step 2: Set up automated engagement and response rules

Unify your inbox across platforms

Many social media managers still handle engagement manually because they want to keep it human. But there are other aspects of engagement that you can automate without losing the human touch.

This starts with the process of tracking your comments, DMs and brand mentions. Instead of tracking everything manually across different networks and profiles, you can automatically collect them in a centralized inbox. This unifies all your engagement opportunities, so nothing falls through the cracks.

Sprout’s Smart Inbox centralizes all your messages from across your connected profiles. This helps you keep up with the latest comments and DMs without having to manually open your social media app. It even lets you manage your responses directly within the inbox.

Automated Inbox Rules further help you manage your responses more efficiently by measuring and categorizing inbound messages. So it’s easy to see which messages you need to prioritize and which ones can wait for a bit.

Build FAQ-style auto-responses for common questions

Quick response times make brands stand out on social. According to the 2025 Sprout Social Index™, nearly three-quarters of consumers expect a response within 24 hours. And 73% will even buy from a competitor if a brand doesn’t respond on social.

But manually answering every message or question slows you down. While this keeps your brand human, it means people have to wait longer even for a generic question. That’s the part of engagement you can automate, giving you more time to focus on interactions that need a more tailored response.

Sprout’s Bot Builder lets you create chatbots and automate responses for frequently asked questions. This streamlines your X (Twitter) and Facebook automation efforts to speed up responses and field routine customer care enquiries.
